## Overview

This thesis investigates two approaches to developing higher-order
shock-capturing schemes based on Roe’s approximate Riemann solver.

The first approach increases the order of the left and right state
reconstruction using weighted essentially non-oscillatory (WENO)
methods. These reconstructed states are used in both the average
and diffusive contributions to the numerical flux.

The second approach applies higher-order central differencing to
the average-flux contribution while retaining higher-order
reconstruction for the diffusive contribution.

Both approaches are evaluated by solving the unsteady,
one-dimensional compressible Euler equations for four
Riemann-problem configurations.

## Research Background

This work was completed in 2021 for the Master of Science in
Engineering program in Mechanical Engineering at the University
of Alabama in Huntsville.

**Author:** Joshua A. Fowler  
**Department:** Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering

The numerical solver was developed from scratch to investigate
how reconstruction and flux formulation affect solution accuracy,
numerical diffusion, and stability.

## Methods Investigated

The thesis develops and examines:

- Finite-volume discretization of the compressible Euler equations.
- Roe’s approximate Riemann solver.
- The Harten–Hyman entropy fix.
- MUSCL reconstruction.
- Third-order and fifth-order WENO reconstruction.
- Higher-order central-differencing modifications.
- Explicit temporal discretization, including an SSP Runge–Kutta method.

## Benchmark Problems

The methods are evaluated using four configurations:

1. Modified Sod shock tube.
2. Blast wave.
3. Shock collision.
4. Stationary contact wave.

The comparisons examine how the schemes resolve shocks,
contact discontinuities, and other high-gradient features.

## Main Findings

For the configurations examined, increasing the order of
reconstruction reduced numerical diffusion and improved the
resolution of high-gradient regions.

The alternative approach using higher-order central differencing
in the average-flux contribution produced unstable behavior and
large oscillations in high-gradient regions for most test cases.

The thesis discusses these results in the context of the
interaction between reconstruction, numerical dissipation,
and flux formulation.

## Related Software

The Euler solver has been implemented independently in several
scientific computing languages:

- [MATLAB — HighOrderEuler-MATLAB](https://github.com/josh-fowler-hub/HighOrderEuler-MATLAB)
- [C++ — HighOrderEuler-Cpp](https://github.com/josh-fowler-hub/HighOrderEuler-Cpp)
- [Python — PyHighOrderEuler](https://github.com/josh-fowler-hub/PyHighOrderEuler)
- [Julia — HighOrderEuler.jl](https://github.com/josh-fowler-hub/HighOrderEuler.jl)

These repositories provide related implementations. Their
current contents may differ from the software version used
for the original thesis.
